title: Lin et al. (2018) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False for each statement. Check the explanation against its linked source segment, paying attention to the study population, measurement timing, and limits of observational evidence.

items.prompt: In the United States, fewer than one in ten people getting divorced were aged 50 or older in 1990, but that share exceeded one in four by 2010.
items.explanation: The rising gray divorce rate and population aging increased older adults' share of all people getting divorced. These figures describe the age composition of divorcees, not the probability that an older married person will divorce.

items.prompt: The earlier study by Karraker and Latham used a sample representative of all married older adults, regardless of their initial health.
items.explanation: That study selected couples who were physically healthy at the outset. Its findings therefore could not be generalized to all married older adults at risk of gray divorce.

items.prompt: Longer life expectancy was proposed as one explanation for rising gray divorce because it lowers the chance that marriage ends through death and extends exposure to the risk of divorce.
items.explanation: This was one of the explanations proposed by Uhlenberg and Myers: longer lives leave marriages exposed to divorce risk for longer. It is a proposed demographic explanation, not a causal effect established by this study.

items.prompt: In the earlier study of initially healthy middle-aged couples summarized in the article, only the husband's illness onset was positively associated with divorce; the wife's illness onset was unrelated to it.
items.explanation: The article summarizes the opposite pattern from Karraker and Latham: the wife's illness onset was positively associated with divorce, whereas the husband's was unrelated to divorce risk. This describes the cited study, not the adjusted findings of Lin and colleagues.

items.prompt: The AHEAD and CODA cohorts were retained in the final analysis because their members were aged 50–64 when they entered the study.
items.explanation: These cohorts entered the HRS at age 68 or older. They were excluded because gray divorce most often occurs between ages 50 and 64; the analysis focused on the HRS and War Baby cohorts.

items.prompt: An empty nest may reduce household burdens, but it may also remove the barrier to divorce provided by resident children and expose relationship strains.
items.explanation: The authors outline two possible pathways: more time together with fewer burdens, or greater exposure of marital strains without resident children as a buffer. These are competing expectations, not a finding that the transition inevitably causes divorce.

items.prompt: The sampling weights adjusted for unequal selection probabilities for Black and Hispanic respondents and Florida residents, as well as nonresponse and sample attrition.
items.explanation: The authors used HRS sampling weights to account for unequal selection, nonresponse, and attrition. Weighting does not mean every possible source of selection bias has been eliminated.

items.prompt: Couples were always excluded if only one spouse was interviewed or if the spouses' reports differed.
items.explanation: When only one spouse responded, the researchers used that spouse's report. In rare cases of inconsistent reports, they used the wife's information.

items.prompt: Teen marriage was coded when either the wife or the husband was under age 20 at the start of the current marriage.
items.explanation: This time-invariant marital biography indicator was coded 1 if either spouse was younger than 20 when the couple married.

items.prompt: The couple's age homogamy measure was defined as the husband's age minus the wife's age and treated as time invariant.
items.explanation: The husband's age itself varied over time, whereas the age difference between spouses was treated as a time-invariant covariate.

items.prompt: Home ownership and assets were time-invariant variables measured only at the first interview, and their values were entered from the same interview wave as divorce.
items.explanation: Both economic measures were time varying and lagged by one interview wave, or two years, to place them before divorce. Establishing this temporal order does not by itself establish causation.

items.prompt: The bivariate estimates were weighted but the multivariate estimates were unweighted, so the two analyses used different population weighting.
items.explanation: The authors applied baseline sampling weights to both the bivariate and multivariate estimates.

items.prompt: All event-history models included interview-year dummy variables to account for period effects.
items.explanation: Each model included interview-year indicators to account for changes over calendar time, given that gray divorce had become more common than in earlier decades.

items.prompt: The researchers estimated survival probabilities by marital duration only for all couples pooled together, without distinguishing first marriages from remarriages.
items.explanation: They estimated survival probabilities separately for first marriages and remarriages to assess a possible interaction between marriage order and duration. This analytic choice alone does not establish that an interaction exists.

items.prompt: The HRS attempted to contact respondents again after a missed wave, and the researchers included some couples who returned in later waves.
items.explanation: Recontact allowed the researchers to use data from some returning couples. They still acknowledged that couples who divorced might have been more likely to drop out, potentially biasing the findings.
